title: `def` defines a function, and calling it starts its execution.
body: The line `def add(a, b):` is code that declares the function. The function body does not execute immediately upon encountering that line. Actual execution begins when the function is called—for example, `add(2, 3)`—with parentheses following the function name.
detail: A "def" line is not a line that executes a function; rather, it prepares the function so that it can be called later. Actual execution begins on the call line, where parentheses follow the function name, as in `add(2, 3)`. When reading code, distinguish between the definition and the call, and consider that the flow within the function restarts each time it is called.

title: A parameter is the name of an input used within a function.
when_to_show: When looking at where the function call arguments go
body: In `def double(x):`, `x` is a parameter. When you call `double(4)`, the argument 4 is assigned to the parameter `x`. Inside the function, you can use 4 under the name `x`.
detail: A "parameter" is the name given to an input value within a function, while an "argument" is the value actually passed when the function is called. In the case of `double(4)`, the value 4 is assigned to the parameter `x` and is used as `x` within the function body. If there are default values or keyword arguments, you should list the final values for each parameter in a table to ensure you don’t lose track of the flow.

title: The `return` statement returns a value and terminates the function's execution.
body: The `return` statement returns the function’s result to the calling location. When `return` is executed, the function’s execution ends. Therefore, even if there is code with the same indentation level below `return`, it may not be executed.
detail: A `return` statement returns a value created within a function to the point where it was called and terminates the function’s execution at that moment. Since the line following the `return` statement may not be executed, its position is important. Unlike `print`, it should be understood as passing a value to be used in subsequent calculations or assignments, rather than a value displayed on the screen.

title: "print" and "return" serve different purposes.
when_to_show: When You Confuse `print` and `return` Inside a Function
body: `print` and `return` serve different purposes. This card helps you distinguish between screen output and function results within a function’s scope. A `print` statement inside a function displays a value on the screen.
detail: When reading a function, you must keep `print` and `return` separate. Write `print` in the output field, and write `return` in the field for the value returned to the caller. Even if only `print` is executed within a function, the call result may be `None`. On a line like `result = func()`, check the value displayed on the screen and the value stored in `result` separately.

title: Variables within a function are evaluated first during the function's execution.
when_to_show: When reviewing local variable, scope, function
body: Variables inside a function are tracked first within the function’s execution. Rather than providing a deep theoretical explanation of scope, this card is a “Function Scope Reading Card” that tells you which lines to read and in what order when dealing with real-world problems.
detail: Variables inside a function are first tracked in the inner scope of the function. Even if there is a variable with the same name outside the function, you should not assume that an assignment inside the function immediately changes the value of the outer variable. It is safest to clearly distinguish between the value of the outer variable before the call, the value passed as a parameter, changes to the local variables inside the function, and the value that remains in the outer scope after the return statement.

title: Variables with the same name are treated differently depending on whether they are inner or outer variables.
body: There may be an `x = 10` outside the function and an `x = 3` inside it. In this case, it’s easy to make a mistake by assuming that the `x` inside the function and the `x` outside are always the same. The `x` that is newly assigned inside the function is read first as the value used in the function’s internal flow.
detail: If variables with the same name exist both inside and outside a function, they can behave as if they were different variables. Even if you execute `x = 3` inside a function, the outer `x` may remain unchanged. When reading code, check which scope the current line is in, where the name was defined, and whether the output is the inner value or the outer value.

title: The result of a function call can be stored in a variable.
when_to_show: When looking at the form `result = func(...)`,
body: `result = add(2, 3)` means that the value returned by the `add` function is stored in `result`. The value calculated inside the function is returned, and that return value becomes the right-hand side of the assignment statement.
detail: The result of a function call can be used as the value on the right-hand side of an assignment statement. In `result = add(2, 3)`, the return value of `add` is stored in `result`. Even if the variable names inside and outside the function are different, the flow is connected via the `return` statement. Distinguish whether the result of a call is discarded, stored in a variable, or passed to another function.

title: If there is no `return` statement, the result of the call may be `None`.
body: If a Python function ends without encountering a `return` statement, it usually returns `None`. Even if you use `print` inside the function, the return value may be `None` if there is no `return` statement. If you run `print(result)` after `result = hello()`, the output from inside the function and the output of `result` may appear separately.
detail: Functions that end without a `return` statement typically return `None` as the result of the call. Even if a `print` statement is executed inside a function and displays a value on the screen, the value stored in `result = func()` may be `None`. When reading code, distinguish between what a function displays and what it returns, and note that `None` can behave like `False` in conditional statements.

title: A conditional `return` statement can terminate a function early
when_to_show: When reviewing early return, if, return
body: If an `if` condition inside a function evaluates to `True` and the `return` statement is executed, the function terminates immediately. Subsequent `return` statements or assignments may not be executed.
detail: A `return` statement without a condition can terminate a function prematurely. If the `if` condition evaluates to `True` and the function encounters a `return` statement, any subsequent assignments or other `return` statements may not be executed. In a function with multiple `return` statements, the conditions are evaluated from top to bottom based on their actual values, and the function must follow the first return path that is executed.

title: If you pass a list to a function, changes made within the function may be retained.
when_to_show: When a list is appended within a function
body: If you pass a list to a function and then call `items.append('a')` within the function, the same list object is modified, so the change may be visible from outside the function as well.
detail: If you pass a list to a function and then perform operations that modify its contents—such as `append` or `pop`—the changes may still be visible from outside the function even after it has finished executing. The behavior of directly modifying the list object differs from the behavior of creating a new list and returning it. You must distinguish between modifying the value and returning a new value.

title: Assigning a value to a numeric variable inside a function does not change its value outside the function.
when_to_show: When changing a numeric parameter inside a function
body: Even if you execute `n = n + 1` inside a function, the outer variable `x` is not automatically updated. `n` is the parameter name used inside the function, and `x` is the outer variable. For a function to pass a new value to the outside, it must return the value (e.g., `return n`), and the outside must reassign it (e.g., `x = add_one(x)`).
detail: For values such as numbers, even if you set `n = n + 1` inside a function, the outer variable `x` is not automatically updated. Parameters inside a function are tracked by their inner names first; to change the outer value, you usually need to use `return` to return a new value and then store it again. Writing the values before and after the call separately helps reduce confusion.

title: Nested functions require the inner `def` to be called as well.
when_to_show: When reviewing nested function, def, call
body: Even if there is another `def` inside a function, the inner function must be called in order to execute. When the outer function is called, the inner function definition may be set up, but unless there is a call such as `inner()`, the body of the inner function will not execute.
detail: In nested functions, the inner `def` statement merely prepares the function; its body is executed only when it is called separately. Just because the outer function is executed does not mean the inner function is automatically executed. When reading code, you should identify the outer and inner calls separately and also check whether the inner function accesses outer variables.

title: "global" indicates that the outer variable will be modified directly.
body: The `global x` keyword indicates that the function will use the outer `x` variable rather than creating a new local variable named `x` within the function.
detail: The `global` keyword indicates that the function will directly access the outer variable rather than creating a new local variable. Therefore, when a function containing `global` is called, the value of the outer variable may change. Generally, returning a value using `return` is safer, so `global` is considered a warning sign that makes it difficult to trace the flow of the program.

title: The default argument is used when no argument is provided.
when_to_show: When you see code like `def greet(name='Guest')`,
body: If a function parameter has a default value, you can omit the argument when calling the function. If you call `greet()` from `def greet(name='Guest')`, `name` becomes `Guest`; if you call `greet('Mina')`, `name` becomes `Mina`. Default values are important for determining what values are actually passed to parameters when reading a function call.
detail: The default value is the value assigned to a parameter when the argument is omitted during a function call. Even though `greet()` and `greet('Mina')` call the same function, the final value of the parameter differs. When reading code, it is helpful to clearly distinguish between the actual value provided, the default value used when the argument is omitted, and the value specified using a keyword for each function call.

title: Key-value arguments pass values by name.
body: Key-value arguments are a way of passing arguments by parameter name rather than by position. As in `greet(age=10, name='Mina')`, even if the order changes, the value is assigned to the corresponding parameter as long as the name matches.
detail: Keyword arguments pass values based on parameter names, not position. As in `func(age=10, name='kim')`, even if the order changes, the values are assigned to the corresponding parameters as long as the names match. You must map the keyword arguments in the function call to the parameter list in the function definition, and when default values are provided, you must determine which values have been omitted.

title: The function scope problem is read in four steps
body: For function problems, first check where the `def` statement is located, then find the line where the function is actually called. Second, write down how the arguments are passed to the parameters. Third, follow the local variables and the `return` statement inside the function.
detail: The function scope problem can be broken down into four steps for a systematic approach. First, write down the initial values outside the function and locate the actual call line. Next, describe how the arguments are passed to the parameters, and trace the local variables and the return statement within the function. Finally, check what remains in the outer variables and in the console output after the return statement.
